what_it_does: Materials scientists use a computational method called GW (Green's function Wigner) calculations to predict how electrons behave in crystalline materials by solving many-body quantum equations. These calculations are essential for understanding material properties but demand enormous computational power, limiting researchers to studying only tiny systems. This paper enables GW calculations on exascale supercomputers — the largest machines with billions of billions of floating-point operations per second — by developing new computational methods and optimization strategies. The work demonstrates these methods across different GPU accelerators (AMD's MI250X graphics chips on the Frontier supercomputer and Intel Xe graphics on the Aurora supercomputer), proving the algorithms work efficiently on different hardware architectures. The researchers use a two-level decomposition strategy that carefully choreographs communication between distributed compute nodes to minimize data transfer overhead, a critical bottleneck at supercomputer scale.
